_comment: The sections of security-notes.md: one for each ASVS requirement that asks for a document and nothing else. `sv notes` writes a section for each that applies, headed by its id, with the question in plain words and what `sv` found that bears on it; the owner writes the answer. A section with an answer makes its requirement *documented*, never *checked*: nothing here reads whether the answer is right, or whether the app does what it says. `title` and `asks` share words with the requirement (crates/sv-check/tests/notes.rs reads them against it), `plain` asks the same in one sentence a person who is not a programmer can answer, and is asked first (backlog 0427), `facts` names what `sv` fills in, and `elsewhere` lists every requirement, at any level, whose words mention documentation and that has no section here, with why, so a new one cannot be missed silently.

sections.title: What counts as valid input
sections.asks: For each kind of information people type into the app (names, email addresses, dates, amounts, free text), write down the validation rules: what a valid value looks like, how long it may be, and what the app does with one that is not valid.
sections.plain: For each thing people type into the app (a name, an email address, a date, an amount), what does a good one look like, how long may it be, and what should the app do with one that is wrong?
sections.howToFindOut: Go through every form and every field an API accepts, and for each one write what a good value looks like. The quickest way to find them all is to open each page that has a form and list its inputs.

sections.title: Data items that must make sense combined
sections.asks: Where two or more data items have to agree with each other once combined (a start date before an end date, a city that matches the ZIP code), write down which combinations matter and how the app checks that logical consistency.
sections.plain: Which things people enter have to make sense together (a start date before an end date, say), and how does the app check them?
sections.howToFindOut: Open each form that takes more than one value and list the pairs that have to agree — two dates, a country and a postal code, a quantity and a maximum. For each, try the combination that should be impossible and see whether the app takes it.

sections.title: Business limits
sections.asks: Write down the business logic limits: how many of something one person may create or do, and in how long (per user), and any limits across the whole app (globally), such as a daily total.
sections.plain: How many of something may one person make or do, and in how long? And is there any limit for the whole app, such as a total per day?
sections.howToFindOut: Go through the app as a user and note everything somebody could do repeatedly: create a record, send an invitation, start an export. For each, decide the number that would be too many in a day, and write that down.

sections.title: What files people may upload
sections.asks: For each place people can upload a file: the permitted file types and extensions, the maximum size (including once unpacked, for a zip), and how the app makes a file safe to download again, including what happens when a file looks malicious.
sections.plain: Where people can upload a file: which kinds of file are allowed, how big may one be (unpacked, for a zip), and what does the app do with a file that looks dangerous?
sections.howToFindOut: Open each place the app takes a file and look at what the code accepts today: the extensions it allows, the size limit if there is one, and where the file ends up. Write down what it should be, which may not be what it is.

sections.title: How sign-in is protected against guessing
sections.asks: How the app defends against someone trying many passwords (password brute force) or leaked email and password pairs (credential stuffing): rate limiting, delays, or lockout, and the numbers, such as five failed attempts in fifteen minutes. Say how these controls are configured, and how the app stops an attacker locking a real person out on purpose (malicious account lockout).
sections.plain: After how many wrong passwords in a row does the app slow down or lock the account, and for how long? And how does it stop somebody locking a real person out on purpose? (Say the numbers you want, even if the app does not do it yet.)
sections.howToFindOut: Look in your sign-in code for anything that counts failures — a rate limiter, a lockout, a delay. If you find nothing, that is the answer, and the number to write down is the one you want rather than the one you have.

sections.title: Words not allowed in passwords
sections.asks: A list of context-specific words people may not use in their passwords: the app's name, the organization's name, product names, and other words someone would guess first.
sections.plain: Which words should nobody be allowed to use in a password here, because they are the first anyone would guess (the app's name, your organization's name, your products)?
sections.howToFindOut: Start from the names somebody could guess without knowing you: the app, your organization, your product, the town you are in. Add the obvious variations with numbers on the end.

sections.title: Every way to sign in
sections.asks: If there is more than one way to sign in (a password, a Google or Microsoft account, a code by email, an API key), list all these authentication pathways, and say which security controls apply to each, so they are enforced consistently and one is not weaker than the others.
sections.plain: What are all the ways someone can sign in (a password, a Google or Microsoft account, a code by email, a key for programs), and are they all protected as well as each other?
sections.howToFindOut: Open the sign-in page and list every button on it, then search the code for anywhere else a session is created — an API key check, a magic link, a mobile app, an admin back door. Each one is a pathway, and they should all be as strong as each other.

sections.title: How long someone stays signed in
sections.asks: The session inactivity timeout (how long someone can be away before signing in again) and the absolute maximum session lifetime (how long any session lasts at most), and why those times are right for this app. If they are longer than NIST SP 800-63B suggests, say why.
sections.plain: How long may someone be away before they have to sign in again, how long may anyone stay signed in at most, and why are those times right for this app?
sections.howToFindOut: Find the two numbers in your app's configuration: how long an idle session lasts, and how long any session lasts at most. If you cannot find them, the answer is whatever your framework does by default, and that is the number to write down and then reconsider.

sections.title: Signed in on several devices at once
sections.asks: How many concurrent sessions one account may have at once (a phone and a laptop, say), and what the app does when someone reaches the maximum: sign out the oldest, refuse the new one, or tell the person.
sections.plain: How many devices may one person be signed in on at once, and what happens when they sign in on one more?
sections.howToFindOut: Sign in to the same account from two browsers and see whether both keep working. That tells you what the app does today; write down what it should do.

sections.title: Sign-in shared with other systems
sections.asks: If people sign in through a shared system (single sign-on, SSO, a federated identity provider), list every system that creates or manages their sessions, and how session lifetimes and signing out are coordinated between them, including when to ask for re-authentication.
sections.plain: If people sign in through another system (single sign-on), which systems keep them signed in, and how do they agree on when someone is signed out?
sections.howToFindOut: Only if people sign in through a shared system. List every system that can create a session for your app, and find out what happens in each when somebody signs out of one: often nothing, which is the thing to write down.

sections.title: Who may do what
sections.asks: The authorization rules: which kinds of users may use which functions (function-level: only administrators may open the admin page), and which records each may see or change (data-specific: a person may only open their own notes).
sections.plain: Who may do what in the app: which kinds of people may use which features, and whose records may each one see or change?
sections.howToFindOut: List the kinds of user the app has, then walk through the app as each one and note what they can reach. The pages that only some people should see, and the records that belong to one person, are what these rules are about.

sections.title: Who may see or change each field
sections.asks: Where some fields of a record are more restricted than the record itself, the field-level access rules: who may read and who may write each field, and whether that depends on the record's state or status (a published order's total can no longer be changed).
sections.plain: Where some parts of a record are more private than the rest: who may see each part, who may change it, and does that change once the record is, say, published?
sections.howToFindOut: Take a record with a field not everybody should see — a price, a note, an internal status. Write down who may read it and who may change it, and whether that depends on the record's state.

sections.title: How keys are looked after
sections.asks: The policy for cryptographic keys: where each key is kept, who can reach it, how often it is replaced, and what happens when one may have leaked, following a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57 through each key's lifecycle.
sections.plain: For each secret key the app uses: where is it kept, who can get to it, how often is it replaced, and what happens if it may have leaked?
sections.howToFindOut: List every key the app uses: session signing, encryption at rest, the TLS certificate, anything a provider gave you. For each, write where it lives, who can read it, and what you would do tomorrow if it leaked.

sections.title: Every key, algorithm, and certificate
sections.asks: A cryptographic inventory: every key, algorithm, and certificate the app uses, where each key may and may not be used, and what data each may and may not protect. Keep it updated when one is added or replaced.
sections.plain: What is every key, kind of encryption, and certificate the app uses, and what may each one be used for?
sections.howToFindOut: Look in your .env and your host's secret store, at the certificate on the live site, and at whatever the code calls to hash or encrypt. That is the inventory; write down which data each protects and where it may not be used.

sections.title: Everything the app talks to
sections.asks: All the communication needs of the app: every external service it connects to (payment providers, email, AI services, other APIs) and why, and any place where someone using the app can give it an address that the app will then connect to itself.
sections.plain: What does the app connect to outside itself (payments, email, AI services, other programs), and why? And can anyone using the app give it an address that it will then visit itself?
sections.howToFindOut: Look at your dependency list for anything that calls out — payment, email, AI, maps, analytics — and at the report's own list of outside services. Then add the places where somebody using the app can give it an address it will fetch.

sections.title: How each kind of sensitive data is protected
sections.asks: For each kind of sensitive data the app holds, its protection requirements: whether it is encrypted, how long it is kept (retention), whether and how it may appear in logs, who can see it, and anything the privacy law you follow requires.
sections.plain: For each kind of private information the app keeps: is it encrypted, how long is it kept, may it appear in logs, who can see it, and what does the privacy law you follow require?
sections.howToFindOut: Take each kind of data from the list you made for V14.1.1 and decide four things for it: encrypted or not, kept for how long, allowed in logs or not, and who may see it.

sections.title: How quickly outdated libraries are updated
sections.asks: Time frames for remediation: how soon a third-party library with a known vulnerability is updated, by how serious the vulnerability is (for example, critical within a week), and how often libraries are updated in general.
sections.plain: When a library the app uses turns out to have a security hole, how soon must it be updated, by how serious the hole is (critical within a week, say)? And how often are libraries updated anyway?
sections.howToFindOut: Decide the number of days you would accept between a vulnerability being published and it being fixed, for each level of severity. Start from how bad it would be for this app rather than from what other people write down. Then put the same numbers in stackvet.toml as `[policy] fix-within-days`, so `sv audit` can hold the app's packages to them.

sections.title: Slow or heavy features
sections.asks: Which functionality is time-consuming or resource-demanding (large exports, report generation, AI requests, image processing), and how the app prevents a loss of availability from overusing it: queues, limits per user, timeouts.
sections.plain: Which features are slow or heavy (big exports, reports, AI requests, image processing), and what stops one person's heavy use from making the app unavailable to everyone else?
sections.howToFindOut: Time the slow things: an export, a report, a search over everything, an AI request, anything that resizes an image. Anything a person notices waiting for is what this asks about.

sections.title: What the app logs
sections.asks: An inventory of the logging: which events are logged, in what format, where the logs are stored, who can read them (access), what they are used for, and how long they are kept.
sections.plain: What does the app write in its logs, where are they kept, who can read them, what are they for, and how long are they kept?
sections.howToFindOut: Find where the app's output actually goes — the console, a file, your host's logging, an outside service — and what it writes at each level. Then say who can read it and how long it is kept.

sections.title: Which browser security features the app expects, and what it does without them
sections.asks: Write down the security features a browser must support to use the app safely (such as HTTPS, HTTP Strict Transport Security, and a Content Security Policy), and how the application behaves when a browser does not support one of them: does it warn the user, or block access?
sections.plain: Which safety features must a visitor's browser have to use the app (a secure connection, for one), and what does the app do when a browser lacks one: warn the person, or keep them out?
sections.howToFindOut: List the security headers the app sends (an `sv report` run against the app lists them), then decide, for an old or unusual browser that ignores one, whether the app should carry on, show a warning, or refuse.

sections.title: The time, place, address, or device the app looks at to decide
sections.asks: Write down the environmental and contextual attributes the application uses to make security decisions, such as the time of day, the user's location, their IP address, or their device, and which decisions each one is used in, including those about authentication and authorization.
sections.plain: Does the app ever decide something about safety from the time of day, where someone is, the internet address they come from, or the device they use, and if so, which of those does it look at, and for what?
sections.howToFindOut: Search the code for where it reads the time, the visitor's address, their location, or their browser, and note each place that changes what someone may do or whether they must sign in again.

sections.title: How those factors change a sign-in or a permission: thresholds and actions
sections.asks: In the authentication and authorization documentation, write down how environmental and contextual factors are used in decision-making, beside the function-level, data-specific, and field-level rules: the attributes evaluated, the thresholds for risk, and the action taken at each (allow, challenge, deny, or step-up authentication).
sections.plain: When the app judges a sign-in or a request riskier than usual, what makes it riskier, how risky is too risky, and what happens then: let it through, ask again, refuse, or ask for a second proof of who they are?
sections.howToFindOut: Start from the list written for V8.1.3. For each factor, write the point at which it changes the outcome and what the app does then. If nothing changes the outcome, say that: it is an answer.

sections.title: A plan for moving to new cryptographic standards
sections.asks: Keep the cryptographic inventory, and with it a documented plan for the migration path to new cryptographic standards, such as post-quantum cryptography, so the app can react to future threats: what would be replaced, in what order, and who decides when.
sections.plain: If the ways the app scrambles and signs data had to be swapped for newer ones (as quantum computers may one day require), is there a written plan for what would change, in what order, and who decides?
sections.howToFindOut: Start from the list of cryptography written for V11.1.2. For each entry, note what would replace it and whether the library the app uses already offers the replacement.

sections.title: How many connections to each service, and what happens at the limit
sections.asks: For each service the application uses, write down the maximum number of concurrent connections (for example, a database connection pool's limit), and how the application behaves when that limit is reached, including any fallback or recovery, so the limit does not become a denial of service.
sections.plain: For each service the app connects to (its database, for one), how many connections can be open at once, and what does the app do when they are all in use: wait, give up, or fall back to something else?
sections.howToFindOut: Look in the app's settings for a pool size or a connection limit for each service, often in the database settings or the code that connects. Where none is set, the library's default is the limit; write down which.

sections.title: Timeouts, retries, and releasing what each outside system hands the app
sections.asks: Write down the resource-management strategy for every external system or service the app uses (databases, file handles, threads, HTTP connections): how each resource is released, the timeout settings, failure handling, and where retry logic exists, its retry limits, delays, and back-off. For a synchronous HTTP request, the timeout should be short, and retries off or strictly limited, so delays do not cascade.
sections.plain: For each outside system the app uses, how long does the app wait before giving up, does it try again and how many times, and does it always let go of what it opened (a file, a connection) when it is done or something fails?
sections.howToFindOut: Find each place the app calls a database, another website's API, or opens a file, and look for a timeout and a retry setting beside it. A call with no timeout waits for ever by default in many libraries; write that down too.

sections.title: Which secrets matter most, and when each is rotated
sections.asks: Write down the secrets that are critical for the security of the application (keys, passwords to other services, signing secrets) and a schedule for rotating each, based on the organization's threat model and business requirements.
sections.plain: Which of the app's passwords and keys would do the most harm if someone else had them, and how often is each one replaced with a new one?
sections.howToFindOut: List what the app reads from its environment or its secrets store: the database password, other services' keys, the key that signs sign-in cookies. For each, write who can replace it, how, and how often.

sections.title: The third-party libraries considered risky components
sections.asks: In the application documentation, highlight the third-party libraries considered to be "risky components": ones that are unmaintained, that run with more access than they need, that parse untrusted input, or that the app could not easily replace.
sections.plain: Of the add-on packages the app uses, which ones would you call risky (no longer looked after, handling what strangers send, or hard to replace), and why?
sections.howToFindOut: Go through the dependency list (package.json, requirements.txt, or the like). For each package, look at when it last had a release and what it does with what visitors send. `sv report` lists the known vulnerabilities in each when given the advisory data.

sections.title: The parts of the app with dangerous functionality
sections.asks: In the application documentation, highlight the parts of the application where "dangerous functionality" is used: running other programs, building database queries or file paths from what a user sends, reading uploaded files, or turning stored data back into objects.
sections.plain: Which parts of the app do something that could go badly wrong if misused (running another program, reading uploaded files, building a file path or a database query from what someone typed), and where are they?
sections.howToFindOut: Search the code for where it runs a command, opens a file by a name that came from a request, builds a query by joining text, or loads stored data as objects. Each place you find is one to list.

elsewhere.why: about output encoding for an HTML document; it asks for no documentation
about escaping JavaScript content; it asks for no documentation
asks for the business limits to be implemented as documented: behavior, which the document in V2.1.3 does not show
about how documents from one site can reach another; it asks for no documentation
about file names keeping a document's structure; it asks for no documentation
asks for the documented list of words to be used when a password is chosen: behavior
asks for the brute-force controls to be implemented as documented: behavior, the running-app half of V6.1.1
asks for multi-factor authentication; documentation is needed only for an exception
asks that no sign-in pathway is undocumented, which is a fact about the app, not the document
asks the app to check an identity provider's claims; documentation is needed only for a fallback
asks for the inactivity timeout to be enforced: behavior, the running-app half of V7.1.1
asks for the absolute session lifetime to be enforced: behavior, the running-app half of V7.1.1
asks for sessions shared with an identity provider to behave as documented: behavior
asks that API documentation is not exposed: a fact about the running app
asks for sensitive data to be protected as documented: behavior, the half of V14.1.2 a document does not show
asks that no component is past its documented update time: checked against the app's packages, not the document
asks for defenses against overuse to be implemented: behavior, the half of V15.1.3 a document does not show
asks that logs go only where the log inventory says: behavior, the half of V16.1.1 a document does not show
asks for the documented security events to be logged: behavior
asks for a DTLS key to be managed as documented: behavior, and only for WebRTC
asks for client-side code written so page elements cannot overwrite its variables (DOM clobbering): a coding practice, not a document
about a header on every page the browser renders; "document" here means the page, and `probe.opener-policy-missing` checks it
about which signed-in resources another site can load or embed; "documents" here means files such as images and scripts
asks for an integrity hash on scripts loaded from other sites, which semgrep looks for, and a written decision only where one cannot be used
asks the app to behave as the V3.1.1 section says when a browser lacks a feature: behavior, checked by hand
asks for the adaptive controls V8.1.3 and V8.1.4 describe to be built: behavior, not the document itself
asks each connection to follow the limits the V13.1.2 and V13.1.3 sections set down: behavior, checked by hand
asks for secrets to expire and be rotated as the V13.1.4 section's schedule says: behavior, not the schedule itself
asks for extra protection around what the V15.1.4 and V15.1.5 sections name: behavior, not the list itself
